theme: Pharaoh hardens; Moses discouraged; the plagues begin
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 5:1-7:25. Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh for the first time, and everything gets worse. Read it as the story of a man who obeys God and sees the result make his people’s lives harder, and notice how God responds to Moses’ discouragement.
settingTheScene: You have just left Moses at the burning bush with a commission and a promise. Now he goes to Egypt and puts it to the test. The next several chapters tell the story of the ten plagues, which are the most dramatic series of events in the Old Testament. They are a contest between the LORD and the greatest empire on earth. But before the plagues begin, there is a long scene of disappointment. The first attempt to free Israel does not work. In the process, the question the whole book turns on is made clear: who is the LORD, and will Pharaoh obey him?
observation: Moses and Aaron say to Pharaoh, “Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness” (5:1).
Pharaoh answers, “Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go” (5:2).
Pharaoh makes the labor harder by requiring bricks without straw (5:6-9).
The Israelite foremen blame Moses: “You have made us stink before Pharaoh” (5:21).
Moses complains to God: “O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me?” (5:22).
God answers, “Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh” (6:1), and he says again, “I am the LORD” (6:2, 6, 7, 8).
God makes a series of promises: “I will bring you out…I will deliver you…I will redeem you…I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God” (6:6-7).
But the people “did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery” (6:9). Moses says he has “uncircumcised lips” (6:12).
God says, “I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet” (7:1). He says, “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (7:3).
Aaron’s staff becomes a serpent and swallows the magicians’ serpents (7:10-12). The Nile is turned to blood (7:14-25).
interpretation:
Pharaoh’s first question is the right one. “Who is the LORD?” He does not know, and he will find out. The whole sequence of plagues is the answer. God says over and over that the purpose is that Egypt and Israel will know that he is the LORD (7:5). It is a knowledge that comes through action.

The worsening of Israel’s conditions is a test of Moses’ faith, and it is a test for every believer. Often, when you try to obey God, things get harder before they get better. The people blame Moses. Moses blames God. This is one of the more honest scenes in the Bible. Moses does not hide what he feels. He says, “Why did you ever send me?” And God does not rebuke him. He answers with a restatement of who he is and what he will do.

God’s answer in chapter 6 is the heart of the passage. Listen to the four, or five, “I will” statements: bring out, deliver, redeem, take, and later in verse 8, bring in. This is a gospel in miniature. He will free them from the burden, rescue them from slavery, and redeem them with an outstretched arm. And then comes the covenant goal: “I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God.” The purpose of redemption is relationship. They are rescued in order to belong.

The people cannot hear it. Their spirit is broken. This is another honest detail. Some pain makes it hard to receive good news. God does not scold them for it. He continues to act.

The hardening of Pharaoh is a topic that deserves care. The text speaks of it in several ways. God says he will harden Pharaoh’s heart (4:21; 7:3). Pharaoh’s heart is also described as hardened without any stated agent (7:13), and later Pharaoh hardens his own heart (8:15, 32). The Bible holds these together: God is sovereign over Pharaoh’s will, and Pharaoh is responsible for his choices. Paul will take this up in Romans 9:17-18, saying that God raised up Pharaoh to show his power. You may find this hard. It is worth sitting with the discomfort rather than explaining it away. The first thing to see is that God’s purpose is to reveal who he is, and the second is that Pharaoh was not coerced into evil. He was an oppressor who did what he wanted.
connection: Jesus says to his disciples that “in the world you will have tribulation,” and then, “take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). The four “I will” promises of 6:6-7 are echoed in Jesus’ words in John 10:28 and in Titus 2:14, where he “gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession.” Romans 9:14-24 takes up the question of Pharaoh’s hardening.
application:
Are you discouraged because obeying God made things harder? Take Moses’ complaint to God, as he did. He can bear it.

Memorize Exodus 6:6-7. Use the promises as your own. Notice that they are about God’s action, not yours.

If someone in your life is too broken to hear good news, pray for them and keep showing them love.
prayerPrompts: Bring your complaint about how hard things are to God, honestly.
Ask him to remind you who he is.
Ask for the courage to keep going.
